draft.title: First Nations cultural and intellectual property
card: First Nations art, designs and stories are part of living cultures. Many First Nations businesses sell products based on them, such as paintings, fabric and books.
a legal right that lets the creator of an artwork, design or story control how it is copied and used. A business can take action if someone copies it without permission.
the owner gives another business permission to use the work, on agreed terms and usually for a fee. The owner decides what is allowed.
Protecting these works keeps control with the people they belong to. It can also give a business an edge, because customers can only buy the genuine work from the owner or a licensed seller.
draft.remember: Copyright and licensing let First Nations businesses control their work, which gives them an edge.

a.q: A First Nations design studio lets a clothing company print its artwork on shirts for an agreed fee. What is this arrangement?
opts: Licensing
Outsourcing
Advertising
Differentiation
a.why: The studio owns the artwork and gives permission to use it on agreed terms, for a fee. That is licensing. It is not advertising, because the main point is permission to use the work, not making the product known.
a.clue: The owner gives permission on set terms.

b.q: A business sells artwork painted by a First Nations artist. A rival copies the painting onto cheap mugs without asking. How does copyright help the artist's business?
opts: It lets the artist control and act against the copying
It makes the mugs cheaper to produce for the artist
It stops customers from buying any other artwork
It makes the artist's paintings sell without advertising
b.why: Copyright gives the creator control over how the work is copied and used, so the artist can take action over copying without permission. It does not lower costs. Protecting the work may help the business, but it does not guarantee sales.
b.clue: Think about who controls copying of the work.

b.best: It lets the artist control and act against the copying

problems.detail: The card suggests copyright protects First Nations cultural expressions and keeps control with 'the people they belong to'. In Australia, copyright only protects particular works by identifiable creators that are in material form (painted, written or recorded). It does not protect traditional stories, styles or communally owned cultural knowledge as such. This is a known gap in Australian law, so the card overstates what copyright does.
The remember line says copyright and licensing 'gives them an edge' as a certainty. The card only says protection 'can also give a business an edge'.

The stem says 'A business sells artwork painted by a First Nations artist', then asks about 'the artist's business'. This leaves it unclear whether the seller is the artist's own business or a separate seller, and so who holds the copyright.
The clue 'Think about who controls copying of the work' repeats the word 'control' from the right option, so it gives the answer away.

check.summary: Both answers are clear, but the card overstates copyright: in Australia it protects specific works by individual creators, not traditional cultural expressions, and the remember line drops the card's 'can'. Question b's stem is unclear about whose business it is, and its clue echoes the answer.

proposal.title: First Nations cultural and intellectual property
card: First Nations art, designs and stories are part of living cultures. Many First Nations businesses sell products based on them, such as paintings, fabric and books.

a legal right over a particular work, such as a painting, design or written story, made by an identifiable creator. It lets the owner control how that work is copied and act against copying without permission.
the owner gives another business permission to use the work, on agreed terms and usually for a fee. The owner decides what is allowed.

Copyright has limits. It does not protect traditional styles, stories or knowledge shared by a community. Licences and agreements help keep control, and selling genuine, authorised work can give a business an edge.
proposal.remember: Copyright and licensing help First Nations businesses control their work, which can give them an edge.

a.q: A First Nations design studio lets a clothing company print its artwork on shirts for an agreed fee. What is this arrangement?
opts: Licensing
Outsourcing
Advertising
Differentiation
a.why: The studio owns the artwork and gives permission to use it on agreed terms, for a fee. That is licensing. It is not advertising, because the main point is permission to use the work, not making the product known.
a.clue: The owner gives permission on set terms.

b.q: Kirra, a First Nations artist, runs her own business selling her paintings. A rival copies one of them onto cheap mugs without asking. How does copyright help Kirra's business?
opts: It lets her take action against the copying
It protects her community's whole painting style
It lowers the cost of making her own products
It stops customers buying any other artwork
b.why: Kirra created the painting, so she holds copyright in it and can act when it is copied without permission. Copyright covers particular works, not a traditional style shared by a community, so the style option is wrong. It also does not lower her costs.
b.clue: Copyright covers one particular work, not a whole style.
